beats.text: Nineteen hundred. Sponge divers shelter from a storm off a tiny Greek island. One diver comes back up terrified. He saw bodies on the seabed.
They were bronze statues, from a shipwreck two thousand years old. And among them: a lump of corroded bronze.
Two years later, someone spots a tiny, hand-cut gear inside it. Nothing that complex would be built for another thousand years. Some said: aliens.
For a century, nobody could see what was inside. Then, in two thousand five, X-ray scans looked through the bronze.
But what they found was no alien tech. More than thirty bronze gears. And tiny Greek writing, like a user manual.
So the lump was a machine. Turn a handle, and it showed the sun and the moon, and predicted eclipses.
It was built by Greeks, between a hundred and fifty and a hundred years before Christ.
Today, scientists call it the oldest known analog computer.
No aliens. Just a lump of corroded bronze, and Greek genius.

sources: 1901: sponge divers recover finds from the Antikythera shipwreck (Roman era, c. 60s BC); May 1902: a gear wheel is noticed in a corroded fragment at the National Archaeological Museum, Athens (Spyridon and Valerios Stais). Linda Hall Library, 'Scientist of the Day' (2024); Wikipedia 'Antikythera mechanism'.

More than 30 hand-cut bronze gears; nothing comparable built for another thousand years; dated 150–100 BC; tracked sun and moon, predicted eclipses; X-ray tomography 2005–06. Freeth et al. (2006), 'Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism', Nature 444, 587–591; Live Science (2006); NYT (30 Nov 2006).
'Oldest known analog computer': IEEE REACH; History.com (2025). 'Some said: aliens' = popular ancient-astronaut claim, no evidence.

1900: Symi sponge divers (captain Dimitrios Kontos) shelter from a storm at Antikythera; diver Elias Stadiatis reports 'corpses' on the seabed – they were bronze and marble statues; salvage 1900–1901; gear noticed 1902. Inscriptions described as a 'user's guide' (Freeth et al.). Film: 'A Storm at Sea' (Edison, 1900), illustrative, public domain. Map: Sentinel-2 cloudless 2016 by EOX, CC BY 4.0.
